title: Stimulus transfers can produce stronger electoral than consumption responses when targeting follows political responsiveness
source_unit: Italian municipality-level administrative recipient shares, electoral returns, income/employment distributions, and voter-panel evidence; international comparison for the US-centered program
geography: Italy; comparison mechanism for US fiscal-transfer and political-response analysis

observations.period: 2014–2019; Italian 80 Euro Bonus transfer and subsequent elections

denominator.unit: universe of Italian municipalities and administrative/electoral records; exact municipality count is not stated in the audited introduction pages

incumbent_vote_share_effect_per_recipien.unit: percentage-point Democratic Party vote-share increase per 1 percentage-point rise in recipient share in 2014 relative to 2013

average_municipality_short_run_effect.unit: approximate percentage-point incumbent vote-share increase for an average municipality with 20.15% beneficiaries

five_year_persistence.unit: percentage-point higher Democratic Party vote share in higher-recipient places in 2019

non_durable_consumption_response.unit: percent of bonus spent on non-durables, cited from related consumption evidence

durable_consumption_response.unit: percent of bonus spent on durables, cited from related consumption evidence

poorer_targeting_consumption_gain.unit: percent increase in projected overall consumption response under counterfactual poorer targeting

poorer_targeting_electoral_return_loss.unit: at least percent reduction in projected electoral return under counterfactual poorer targeting

observations.method: Quasi-random geographic variation in recipient shares induced by predetermined municipal income and payroll-employment distributions; difference-in-differences, placebo/pre-trend checks, controls, an eligibility-rule IV, threshold-based design, and a voter panel around salient receipt.
observations.uncertainty: The evidence is from Italy and an international comparison, not a US treatment estimate. The paper is an NBER working paper; the counterfactual is projected from heterogeneous estimates and related consumption evidence. Electoral attribution is supported by timing and panel evidence but remains design- and context-specific.
observations.subgroup: Municipalities and voters by recipient income distribution, excluded low-income versus higher-income groups, and likely bonus-recipient status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local recipient density could correlate with other municipal changes despite the design controls; electoral persistence may reflect salience, party attachment, or other policy channels. Consumption and electoral responses need not come from the same individuals.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER metadata and abstract for Working Paper 33973.
US county purchasing-power and electoral association with a different design and geography.

boundary: This is an international comparison mechanism, not a US estimate. It directly strengthens the program's policy exposure → material response → attribution/electoral response architecture while leaving US transfer design, household-level causal incidence, cultural meaning, and generalization open. Consumption estimates and electoral estimates are not treated as the same respondent outcome.
